P01.sentence: Instructors may prohibit the use of AI in their courses.
Instructors should assign writing in writing-intensive courses to be completed without generative AI.
Generative AI is not permitted in this course.
Students must not use generative AI tools for any work in this course.
Students must not use AI unless the instructor explicitly permits or authorizes it for a specific assignment or purpose.
Students must not use AI at any stage of their work, including brainstorming, drafting, outlining and editing.
Students must complete all submitted work independently, without AI assistance.
Students should not use AI tools in completing course work.
Students may use AI tools where course policy permits it.
Students must not use AI on graded work, assessments, exams or work submitted for evaluation.
Using prohibited AI on assignments is academic dishonesty or misconduct.
Policies describe course rules that ban AI use, and the expectation that students will not use it.
Neither instructors nor students will use AI tools in this course.

P02.sentence: Instructors are encouraged to integrate AI into their teaching and courses where appropriate.
Students are welcome and expected to use generative AI tools in this class.
Instructors should permit and encourage students to use AI responsibly.
Generative AI use is neither encouraged nor prohibited on assignments in this course.
Students may use generative AI tools in this course and on assignments.
Students are encouraged to use generative AI tools to support their learning and work.
Students may use generative AI only if they follow stated conditions, such as attribution, disclosure, or instructor guidelines.
Students may use generative AI freely, with no restrictions and no need to cite or document it.
Students may use generative AI only in limited ways or specific circumstances set by the course.
Students may use AI tools but should do so with caution.
Everyone in the university community is encouraged to explore and experiment with AI responsibly.
Universities state that they support, embrace, or value AI use and responsible experimentation.
Policies describe AI as a helpful tool that can improve students' learning, work quality and efficiency.
The university should promote and encourage AI adoption and responsible use among its members.
Instructors should help students engage with AI, consider its ethical implications, and explore what they can create.

P03.sentence: Instructors should limit or avoid generative AI use, including in introductory courses, when it might undermine learning outcomes.
Students are discouraged from using generative AI tools unless the instructor directs or explicitly allows it.
Students are discouraged from using AI tools to generate content such as text, code, images or audio that ends up in their work.
Students are discouraged from using generative AI tools for coursework, though AI is not banned.
Students are discouraged from using AI as a research or academic source when its output cannot be properly cited or sourced.
Instructors may discourage student use of generative AI by encouraging other tools.
Students should use AI cautiously, selectively and thoughtfully, not as a shortcut or a replacement for their own learning.
Generative AI use is discouraged where it is not suited to the task or leads to excessive reliance.
The institution is reluctant to promote or endorse AI tools and systems.

P04.sentence: Instructors may decide whether and how generative AI is used in their own courses, from prohibiting it to encouraging it.
Policies state that the instructor or faculty member has the authority and discretion to decide AI use in a course.
Instructors should decide, define and develop a clear AI policy suited to their course.
Instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course-level AI policy.
Instructors may set different AI rules for different assignments within the same course.
Instructors should consider and provide assignment-level AI guidance rather than only a course-wide rule.
Instructors may adopt or adapt the provided sample AI syllabus statements to fit their course.
Instructors may prohibit AI use entirely or strictly restrict it in their courses.
Universities should preserve faculty autonomy and avoid imposing one-size-fits-all AI rules.
Policies state that assignments will specify whether and how AI tools may be used, and students will be informed.
Instructors must state for each assignment whether AI use is allowed and how.
Instructors should state clearly to students whether and how AI may be used.
Students may use generative AI only on assignments or in ways the instructor permits.
Students must follow the AI usage rules set for each assignment by the instructor or syllabus.
Students must not use AI in ways the instructor does not allow.
Teaching assistants and consultants must follow the instructor's AI decisions and expectations.
Policies leave decisions about misuse and consequences to the instructor's course policy.
Policies warn that AI rules differ across courses, instructors, disciplines and assignments, with no single approach.
The university sets no single AI policy and leaves decisions on AI use to faculty.

P05.sentence: Universities offer sample syllabus statements and templates that range from prohibiting AI to permitting it freely.
Instructors may choose one of the offered policy options or levels for their course or individual assignments.
Policies describe named tiers of AI use, from no AI, to limited or conditional use, to open or encouraged use.
Instructors should select one of the AI use levels or policy options for their course or assignments.
The institution should develop a clear, consistent menu or tier system of AI use policies for instructors.
Instructors should clearly state in the syllabus and assignments which AI uses are permitted at each level.
Instructors may use icons, color labels, tables or scales to show the permitted AI level for each assignment.
Students are informed that each assignment states its AI level, from no AI to full AI collaboration.
Tier frameworks help instructors communicate to students what AI use is acceptable.
Instructors must specify an AI use category for each assignment, activity or course.
Students may use AI only for the limited tasks or conditions the instructor specifies.
Students may use AI freely or extensively where the policy is open.
Students must not use AI on assignments or assessments designated as no-AI.
Frameworks such as the AI Assessment Scale, traffic lights and numbered levels classify AI use, from none to full.

P06.sentence: Students should assume AI use is not permitted when the instructor has not explicitly allowed it.
When a syllabus or assignment is silent on AI, the default is that AI use is not allowed.
Courses without their own AI policy fall back to the school, department or university default policy.
Instructors must state explicitly in the syllabus or assignment what AI use is allowed and tell students AI is unauthorized otherwise.
If an instructor gives no AI statement, students may use AI but must disclose all use.
Students must not use AI on assignments or coursework unless the instructor explicitly permits it.
Unless permitted to use AI tools, each student is expected to complete each assignment on their own.
Students must get the instructor's permission before using AI in coursework.
Students may use AI only where the instructor permits it, with disclosure or attribution.
Where no policy is given, students may use AI tools unless specifically prohibited, and individuals decide for themselves.
When no policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed; substantive AI use requires prior approval.
Instructors will assume students have not used AI except in the explicitly allowed cases.
Teaching assistants and staff must not use AI in their roles unless the instructor says otherwise.
Unauthorized AI use is cheating, plagiarism or academic dishonesty and a violation of integrity policy.

P07.sentence: Instructors should check which tools students use contain AI and state in the syllabus whether grammar checkers, Grammarly, and similar embedded tools are allowed.
Instructors should give students specific guidance on which embedded or everyday tools are acceptable and help them recognize when AI is involved.
Students must not use AI writing assistants or editing tools such as Grammarly, Quillbot, and Wordtune in coursework.
Students should not use embedded, built-in, or plug-in AI tools for core assignments or to generate or heavily change text.
Students may use incidental or embedded tools, such as autocomplete, search features, and code completion, without disclosure or penalty.
Students must turn off or restrict AI features when a ban applies, and must confirm and limit what data AI tools can access.
Policies warn that AI agents and browser plugins can act on students' behalf, such as answering quizzes and discussion posts.
Policies note that AI features are built into many common tools and applications, such as word processors, Google and Microsoft products, and coding software, often without clear labeling.
Autonomous AI agents are prohibited, and agentic AI used to complete assessments without human interaction is cheating.
The university may block or disable AI tools, such as plugins and companion tools, on managed machines.

P08.sentence: Instructors should teach students foundational skills without AI first, then allow or introduce AI once those basics are mastered.
Instructors should allow AI such as tutoring or programming help in advanced courses, and policies should give fewer AI restrictions at higher course levels.
Instructors may set AI use as excluded or permitted at different stages of an assignment, which scaffolding helps clarify.
Students may use AI only after they have practiced or mastered the essential skills, having first worked without it.
Students must not use AI during the peer review stage or on the final draft.

P09.sentence: Instructors must include a statement or policy on generative AI use in every course syllabus.
Programs, units and administrators should set and communicate AI expectations and syllabus requirements for faculty and students.
Instructors should include an AI statement or policy in their course syllabus.
Instructors should clearly communicate to students their expectations on whether and how AI may be used.
Instructors must clearly tell students what AI use is allowed and not allowed in their course.
Instructors should be specific in their AI policy, naming permitted and prohibited uses, tools, examples, rationale, and citation or disclosure rules.
Policies state that clear AI statements help students understand expectations and that missing guidance causes confusion.
Instructors should communicate AI policies early, at course start, and often, both in writing and orally.
Instructors may choose their own approach to AI, may add optional policy statements, and may repeat policies elsewhere.
Instructors should not leave AI expectations ambiguous or assume students already know the rules.
Instructors should state AI expectations in assignment instructions or descriptions, not only in the syllabus.
Instructors must state AI expectations in assignment instructions, marking where AI use is permitted or required.
Instructors should remind students of the AI policy repeatedly, for each assignment and throughout the semester.
Policies note that unclear or absent AI statements make it hard to address academic misconduct.

P10.sentence: Students should ask their instructor about course AI rules and unclear expectations, and check the syllabus, at the start of the course.
Students must seek clarification from the instructor about AI policies before starting their work.
Instructors should encourage students to ask questions about AI use and explain how and whom to ask when unsure.
Students who are unsure whether an AI use is allowed should ask their instructor before using it.
Students who are unsure should ask the instructor before submitting their work.
Students must ask their instructor for clarification when unsure, before using AI; it is their responsibility.
When unsure whether AI use is allowed, students should avoid using AI or assume it is not allowed.
Graduate students should discuss acceptable AI use with their advisors or committee, and must do so where required.
When unsure, students should err on the side of full disclosure of their AI use.
Staff and others who are unsure about AI use should consult their supervisor, unit leadership, or IT.
Students are welcome to contact the instructor with questions about AI use.
Policies state that failing to ask is no excuse, that students may have rules clarified, and that unclear use risks harm.

P100.sentence: Instructors may choose not to require documentation or acknowledgement of AI use, and are not expected to catalog incidental uses.
Instructors may restrict basic AI features only when they are central to what the assignment assesses.
Instructors should state which conventional tools, accessibility features, or exceptions are not counted as AI or remain permitted.
Instructors should resist using basic generative AI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants.
Students may use basic spell-check and grammar-check tools built into word processors while writing.
Students need not disclose or document routine uses such as spell-check, grammar correction, or embedded AI features.
Policies state that routine or incidental AI use is common practice, outside the policy's intent, and needs no documentation or acknowledgement.
Policies state that basic spelling and grammar tools are generally not counted as generative AI under the rules.
Users need not disclose AI embedded in larger software or used for minor, routine tasks like grammar editing.

P101.sentence: Instructors must get prior approval before using AI or software to assist with grading, and may use only approved or university-licensed tools.
Students must be able to opt out of AI-assisted grading and have the instructor review their work instead, without penalty.
Instructors must review and correct AI-generated feedback and findings themselves, keeping a human in the loop and remaining responsible for the result.
Grading and assessment of student work with AI requires extra review, consultation or caution before use.
Instructors may use AI to help draft formative feedback, flag patterns and generate ideas, provided they personalize the feedback.
Instructors should not rely on AI as the primary source of feedback, automate full feedback, or use it for grading written work.
Instructors should not use AI to grade or input student work without students' prior approval.
AI feedback is most appropriate for low-stakes or ungraded assignments.
Instructors should create a quality assurance process so AI grading tools produce accurate, explainable and defendable grades, and avoid tools that cannot be validated.
Policies note that AI grading has limits and ethical concerns, though some tools can ease grading, and student data privacy matters.

P102.sentence: Instructors should learn what current AI systems can do and the risks of using them before teaching their course.
Instructors should familiarize themselves with university policies and guidelines on generative AI, reading them in full, before teaching their course.
Instructors should stay informed about AI developments, tools and resources over time and engage in professional development.
Everyone should stay informed about AI advancements, best practices and institutional guidelines, and keep checking as they evolve.
Students should keep up with changes in AI tools, best practices and university or instructor guidance, and check back regularly.
Teaching assistants and staff should stay informed about evolving AI developments, best practices and training.
Students must stay informed about AI developments and university policies and norms for AI use.
Administrators should keep up with AI reports, laws, regulations and policies.
Everyone should keep abreast of changes in the law, including copyright law, affecting AI use.
Everyone should stay informed about AI, learn about its benefits and risks, and review university policies and resources.
Everyone must stay informed about AI developments, best practices and applicable policy.
Policies state that staying informed about AI and learning about it is valuable, and offer resources for doing so.

P103.sentence: Instructors who implement a chatbot in their course should use the provided disclosure statement.
Meeting organizers must tell participants if AI tools will be used in meetings or shared engagements.
A warning about proper AI use and user responsibilities must be displayed in the interface when interactive AI use begins.
Institutions should tell people how and why AI is used, including where it affects them, and be open about its use.
Institutions must disclose AI use to affected stakeholders when AI is used in decision-making processes.
Users have the right to know when they are working with AI, and AI use is disclosed to those affected.
Chatbots and AI chat assistants must disclose their scope, non-official status, and potential for incorrect information, and AI must not be presented as human.
The university commits to transparency in AI use, with processes and criteria that are clear and accessible to users.
Individuals should be informed when AI-enabled tools are being used.
Policies warn that applications are not always clear about when users are interacting with AI, so students may not know.

P104.sentence: Students may use AI tools to find, search for and research sources and information on their topic.
Students may use AI to summarize research and generate annotated bibliographies.
Students should verify that sources found with AI tools are legitimate.
Students should use AI tools as a place to start their search for information.
Instructors may use AI to support literature exploration or summary.

P105.sentence: Instructors may permit AI summarization of readings or content they have provided, as set in course policies.
Students may use AI to summarize readings, articles and sources to get an overview and aid understanding.
Students must not use AI to summarize or contextualize assigned readings or source materials.
Policies describe summarizing and condensing documents or readings as a use of AI, or say it is beneficial.
Students should not use AI to do the readings, replace reading course materials, or synthesize learning from them.
Students may use AI to summarize sources only with instructor approval, or for the student's own or supplementary materials.
Students must not use AI to summarize or respond to readings unless the instructor explicitly permits it.
Students may use AI to summarize readings if they write their own synthesis and cite accordingly, or verify the summary.

P106.sentence: Students may use AI to generate images, illustrations, figures, and other visuals for their assignments.
Students may submit multimedia assignment material containing AI-generated images, audio, music or video if the use is properly documented.
Students may use AI to generate preliminary visual concepts, design ideas, slide layouts, or presentation structures.
Students may use AI to generate non-technical concept illustrations only with the course instructor's permission.

P107.sentence: Instructors may permit AI only for specific tasks or assignments and should clearly state those limits.
Users must get prior approval or review from the relevant university body before using certain AI tools or data.
Students must consult their advisor, committee chair or faculty mentor and get approval before using AI in research or thesis work.
Instructors must approve AI use before it is allowed in their classes.
Students must get instructor permission before using AI for coursework.
Students may use AI only for specific tasks or assignments that the instructor has authorized or listed.
Students must explain or submit, in writing, how they plan to use AI before using it.
Students may use AI if the instructor gives permission in advance.
Students must not use AI beyond the listed purposes or without authorization.
Students should get explicit instructor permission before using AI.
Staff and faculty must consult a supervisor, administrator or chair before using AI, including non-approved tools.
Students should discuss with the instructor in advance how and why they plan to use AI.
TAs and staff must not use AI without the course instructor's authorization and should use it only for listed tasks.
Students are prohibited from using generative AI in all coursework.
Instructors approve AI use based on how appropriate it is and its educational value.
Policies state that AI use in the course will be limited and specific.

P108.sentence: There is no single university-level syllabus statement about generative AI use.
The university has no university-wide or single AI policy.
Existing university policies, such as academic integrity rules, already apply to AI use without AI-specific clauses.
The university deliberately has no single AI policy, leaving AI decisions to instructors and disciplines because needs and contexts vary.

P109.sentence: Instructors should align their course AI policies with their department's or program's policies, guidance and disciplinary standards before the course begins.
Instructors should discuss AI use and expectations with department colleagues, chairs and peers, and work with them to reach shared approaches.
Departments and academic units should discuss, encourage and facilitate consistent AI approaches and statements among faculty.
Instructors should discuss and agree with department colleagues on appropriate penalties for unauthorized AI use.
Instructors should coordinate AI expectations across course sequences, shared curricula and graduate committees so students meet consistent expectations.
Instructors should develop shared syllabus language specific to the discipline or course.
Faculty and administrators should hold ongoing department conversations about appropriate penalties for unauthorized AI use.
Programs can encourage teaching assistants to connect with supervising faculty so student AI use complies with class guidelines.
Faculty are expected to follow the agreed syllabus learning outcomes.
Institutions must ensure students receive consistent, clear information about permissible AI use across syllabi, assignments and university communications.
Policies state that appropriate AI use differs across disciplines, courses, programs and contexts.
Policies note that students are confused by differing AI rules across courses, and consistent language clarifies expectations.
Policies state that this guidance supplements or sits alongside other institutional AI policies and guidelines.

P11.sentence: Students are told that other courses and instructors may have different AI policies, so expectations should be checked for each course.
Instructors should tell students that AI policies differ between courses and write course-specific policy statements.
Instructors are told that students face varying AI policies across courses and may wrongly assume other courses' rules apply in theirs.
Students are responsible for conforming to the AI expectations of each course they take.
This course's AI policy applies only to this course.
Students must not treat AI permission granted in one course or assignment as approval to use AI in other courses or assignments.
Permitted uses of generative AI may change over time.
Policies state that AI rules and permitted uses vary between courses, instructors and assignments, and what is acceptable in one may be a violation in another.

P110.sentence: Sample AI syllabus statements are available to instructors on university resource pages.
Instructors may use, edit and adapt the provided sample syllabus statements for their own courses.
The institution provides sample syllabus language and templates for instructors to use.
Instructors should choose and adopt one of the provided sample statements or templates for their syllabus.
Instructors should modify or tailor the sample statements to fit their own course.
Sample statements cover a range of positions, from allowing to restricting or prohibiting AI use.
Instructors are offered tools, guides and resources to help them draft their own AI policy.
Instructors may browse policies and statements from other institutions and educators for ideas.
The institution should host or provide sample syllabus statements and templates for instructors.
Instructors may write their own AI policy instead of using a template.
If a provided university statement is used, it must appear in the syllabus exactly as written.
Instructors should include a statement on AI use in their course syllabus.
Instructors should discuss the AI policy and its reasons with students and keep the conversation going.
Instructors should state, per assignment, the acceptable level of AI use, using assignment templates.
Students may use generative AI tools in the course where the instructor permits it, with attribution.
Consistent syllabus language helps students understand their responsibilities across courses.
Students should not use GenAI tools to summarize, generate or interpret thoughts in their work.

P111.sentence: Instructors may consider integrity pledges or statements that AI was not used as an additional option.
Units and universities should consider developing, adopting or altering an honor code or pledge.
Students must sign an academic integrity agreement or AI contract and agree to abide by its terms at the start of the course or term.
Instructors should have students sign an honor code, integrity pledge or statement of understanding at the start of the course.
Instructors should discuss academic integrity with students at the start of the class.
Instructors or supervisors must obtain acknowledgement from students that they understand the expectations set for them.
Students have already signed the Honor Code pledge.
Students must attest, pledge or affirm with each submission that the work is their own and that they attribute any tools and sources used.
Students should include a statement with their work, such as an integrity statement, a note on permitted GenAI use, or responsibility for accuracy and originality.
Instructors should include a declaration of honesty or an affirmation that submitted work is the student's own in assignments.
Instructors should have students sign or reaffirm an honor pledge or honor statement on each assignment, test or exam.

P112.sentence: Instructors should model the behavior and standards they expect from their students, including transparent disclosure of AI use.
Researchers should reinforce responsible AI practices with their mentees.
Instructors should model responsible, ethical and transparent use of AI in their own work so students can learn from their example.
Policies state that instructors' transparent and ethical AI use serves as a professional model for students, who take cues from instructors.
Instructors should model curiosity, critical evaluation and adaptability by engaging with generative AI themselves.

P113.sentence: The institution should establish a clear policy on what logging and auditing of AI use takes place.
Instructors should clearly label and advertise assignments where AI usage logs are shared with them.
AI interactions and records could be accessed during formal misconduct investigations.
The institution may monitor AI use for compliance and risk assessment, including through periodic audits of networks and systems.
The institution reserves the right to access, review and audit prompts, outputs and other information on its AI tools.
Individual user interactions with the institution's AI tool are not monitored.

P114.sentence: Users must review the terms and conditions of AI software before using it.
Users whose AI outputs violate others' intellectual property are responsible for the damage and may face disciplinary sanctions.
A person unlinked to the university who causes damage alone answers for it, exonerating the university, and is barred from using the technology there.
Users are personally responsible for their own use of AI tools and for what happens with the accounts or agents they use.
The university is not responsible for personal data, consequences or negligence arising from users' individual use of external or unsanctioned AI tools.
People who accept click-through agreements with university credentials without delegated signature authority may face personal consequences.
Users should not use their university accounts to sign up for AI tools, and staff must not use tools not cleared by InfoSec.

P115.sentence: Policies list AI teaching resources, guidance pages and reading lists available to instructors.
Instructors may draw on sample syllabus statements, disclosure examples and assignment repositories.
Instructors should review university and school AI guidelines before the course.
Administrators should compile and maintain central AI resource portals and tell instructors about them.
Instructors should consult syllabus statement guidance and state their AI expectations clearly to students.
Instructors may share the listed AI resources and citation guides with students and put them in the syllabus.
Instructors should point students to AI literacy guides and student guides to set classroom norms.
Instructors should link their course AI policy to the academic honesty policy or honor code and campus AI guidance.
Policies point students to library and style-guide pages on citing generative AI in APA, MLA and Chicago formats.
Students should consult the named citation or style guide for how to cite and disclose AI use.
Students and faculty should use library databases and approved AI tools and data allowances.
Policies point to academic integrity and misconduct policies, processes and support resources.
Instructors should consult the conduct or academic integrity office when AI misuse is suspected.
Policies point to institutional AI policies, hubs and guidance pages for further information.
Everyone should review the university's AI guidelines and policies.
Policies point students to student guides and library pages on AI.
Policies point to data classification, privacy and security standards for AI use.
People should consult the security, privacy or data offices when unsure about data use with AI.
Students should review the named AI guidelines and resources before using AI.
Students should review the academic integrity policy or contact the named office with questions.
Policies and offices direct researchers to separate guidance on AI in research.
Instructors should contact the named support offices with questions about AI use.
Policies list approved AI tools and where to find them.
Anyone may contact the named office for questions or more information about AI.

P116.sentence: Instructors should include a notice about ethical and responsible AI use in the syllabus.
Instructors should make ethical use a main consideration and ensure AI integration in their class promotes it.
Students must use AI ethically and responsibly when working with it, following academic integrity and honesty guidelines.
Students should use AI thoughtfully, ethically and with originality and attribution while doing their work.
People should be cautious with AI content that has legal, ethical or reputational implications.
Everyone should use AI ethically and responsibly.
Everyone using AI must use it ethically and responsibly.
Students are expected to use AI ethically and responsibly and keep to academic integrity standards.
Instructors should promote, model and encourage ethical and responsible AI use among students.
Staff and researchers should ensure their AI use is ethical and responsible.
Students must use AI ethically and responsibly.
Policies note that ethical AI use requires attention to harm, bias, accuracy and shared values.

P117.sentence: Users must carefully evaluate an AI tool's capabilities and review institutional policies before using it.
Faculty and administrators should adopt AI tools that meet trustworthiness criteria.
Staff should consult department leadership and colleagues before choosing AI tools.
Instructors should tell students which tools and resources are reliable sources of information.
Users should choose AI tools from reputable, legitimate and trustworthy providers.
Users should choose a tool designed for the task and consider whether AI is the most appropriate tool.
Users must verify that a tool has adequate security and is appropriate for their data before using it.
Users should review a tool's terms of service, privacy policies and data handling practices before using it.
Users should research or critically evaluate a tool, including its reliability and bias, before choosing it.
Users should be cautious of claims made by vendors and product providers.
Policies offer frameworks and guidance to help users evaluate and select AI tools.

P118.sentence: Instructors should weigh AI's educational value, benefits, risks, ethics and their own values before deciding whether to use it in teaching.
Students should weigh the benefits, risks and ethics of AI, and judge whether it is appropriate, before using it for a task.
Everyone using AI should weigh its potential benefits and risks, and consider its impacts, before and while using it.
Decide whether to use AI deliberately, considering necessity, resource cost and goals; availability alone does not justify use.
Policies state that students should make informed, intentional choices about when and how to use AI.
Policies state that whether and how AI use is acceptable depends on the specific use, and that people may make informed decisions or use it for personal exploration.

P119.sentence: Students should confirm what is acceptable before using AI tools for resumes, cover letters, and interviewing.
Students may use AI to prepare for careers, such as exploring occupations and skillsets, resumes, cover letters, and job interviews.
Students may use AI for everyday personal tasks, such as deciphering email tone, creating recipes, and planning meals.
Students should personalize and customize their application materials to stand out.
Policies warn that application reviewers who suspect or can tell AI was used may count it against the application.
Occasional personal use of university AI resources is acceptable if it does not interfere with university business use.
Policies note that generative AI can be a good starting point for research.

P12.sentence: Instructors may allow AI support for researching problems and explaining concepts.
Students may use AI to explain, clarify, or give alternative explanations of difficult concepts and course material.
Students may use AI to find information, background knowledge, or an overview of a topic, like a search engine or reference source.
Students may use AI as a personal tutor or learning partner.
Students are encouraged to use AI wisely as a supplementary resource that deepens their own learning and understanding.
Instructors should encourage or assign students to use AI as a Socratic tutor or to explore and learn course topics.
Students must not use AI chatbots to get answers to conceptual questions about course content at the most restrictive level.
Policies note that AI can act as a tutor, study aid, or Socratic questioner for students.

P120.sentence: Students should confirm AI output is not a direct copy of existing work and cite the original sources.
Students must check that AI-generated content is not plagiarized and verify original sources before using it.
Students must not use AI to generate bibliographies, references or citations, and must do their own research.
Policies warn that AI output can plagiarize or misrepresent sources and give unclear attribution, false citations, or summaries.
Students should not submit or lightly edit AI text that closely mirrors existing sources.
Students must not leave AI-generated citations uncorrected or fail to notice that AI edited quotes and paraphrases.
Policies warn that AI tools use existing sources without citation, risking plagiarism or copied content.

P121.sentence: Instructors and departments should increase human interactions in their courses.
Instructors are encouraged to keep feedback and faculty-student engagement human-centered and personal rather than AI-generated.
Students should not use AI tutoring to replace human interaction with instructors or teaching assistants.
Policies warn that overreliance on AI can reduce human interaction, support, and feedback between students and instructors or peers.
Policies state that AI is a supplementary tool, not a replacement for human interaction, relationships, or instructors' guidance.
Instructors should use AI to augment teaching, not replace the presence, expertise, and care of the instructor.
Teaching assistants and staff should not let AI replace the human element needed for reflective conversations, though it may handle mundane questions.

P122.sentence: The university should allocate funding and resources for AI infrastructure, institutional AI tool subscriptions, pilot programs, and secure environments.
The university should establish a dedicated AI research center or institute that supports interdisciplinary collaboration.
The university should explore enterprise AI and privacy-protecting options to secure research and other data.
The university should develop new AI-related certificate programs.
The university should assess over time whether IT services are sufficiently resourced to support AI use.
Policies state the university encourages and supports AI research, education and exploration by faculty and students.
Policies state the university is committed to investing in AI, integrating it across its operations, and leading in AI research.
Policies describe existing AI research groups, labs and coordinating units at the university.
The university should foster and promote interdisciplinary AI research and its application.
Faculty are encouraged to seek grants and support for AI work.
Policies note the university has not yet established a dedicated AI center.

P123.sentence: Instructors should plan, before the course, how they will detect and handle suspected violations of the AI policy.
Instructors should tell students in advance how they will detect or evaluate AI use, including any detection tools such as Turnitin.
Instructors should tell students at the start of the course how AI misuse will be addressed and handled under the applicable misconduct procedures.
Instructors should state the consequences students face for misusing AI.
Instructors should act promptly when AI policy violations occur or are suspected.
Instructors may use AI detection tools.
Policies warn that AI detectors are unreliable and do not prove student misconduct.

P124.sentence: Instructors should make AI expectations transparent and apply them consistently.
Instructors must grant or deny AI permission to all students in a course alike.
Instructors should apply academic misconduct enforcement and grading consistently across students, so similar cases receive similar outcomes.

Instructors should try out generative AI tools themselves before setting course policy.

Instructors should discuss AI and course approaches with colleagues and seek peer support.
Instructors should review the institution's AI guides and teaching resources.
Instructors should reflect on how AI affects their courses, their own views and ethical principles before setting policy.
Instructors should reach out to the teaching and learning center for guidance on AI.
Instructors may use AI-assisted tools, assignment guides and design exercises to build course policies and assignments.
Instructors should run their own assignments and prompts through AI tools to see what the tools produce.
Faculty who teach with AI must be trained.
Support and consultation are available on AI detection, academic integrity and reporting suspected misuse.
Communities of practice, forums and peer events let faculty learn about AI together over time.
Instructors should keep learning about AI over time through ongoing development, talks and courses.
Instructors should share their AI assignments, syllabus statements and approaches with colleagues.

P64.sentence: Students accused of AI misuse should have the opportunity to respond to the allegation and present their explanation or evidence.
Students may appeal an AI misuse decision through the university's appeal process.
Policies state that students receive fair, transparent treatment and due process in AI misuse cases.
Students accused of AI misuse may contest the allegation or defend themselves, including through a meeting with the instructor.
Instructors should notify the student and offer the resolution options available after suspecting AI misuse.
Students can seek support from campus staff, such as Community Standards or the Disability Access Center, when handling an allegation.
Students must submit their written statement within the set deadline after an allegation.
Reports of suspected AI misuse go to the department chair, who gathers information.

P65.sentence: Anyone at the university must submit an AI tool for IT or governance review and get approval before acquiring or using it, even if it is free.
University administration must establish a process to review and approve AI tools and vendors for security, privacy, risk and compliance before adoption or deployment.
Contracts with AI vendors must include data protection, privacy and security terms, and vendors must disclose their AI use.
Policies describe IT or security offices reviewing AI tools for security, privacy, legal and accessibility standards before approval.
AI purchases and subscriptions must follow the university's standard procurement process.
Users should consult IT or Information Security before buying, signing up for or using an AI tool, even a free one.
Instructors must get an AI tool reviewed or approved by IT before requiring it in a course or using it with student work.
Community members may submit requests for new AI tools to be reviewed or integrated.
Staff must go through the standard contracting and procurement process to obtain approval before acquiring AI tools.
University information may be used with AI tools only if the tool is approved for that data type and use.
Approved AI tools must be reviewed again periodically or when they change.
Policies describe ongoing efforts to evaluate AI tools and note limits of current agreements and detection tools.
The university may block, restrict or prohibit unauthorized or risky AI tools.
Vendors and third parties must not use university data to train or improve AI models unless explicitly authorized.
Policies state that vendor contracts exist or restrict training on university data, or that data entered into AI products is retained.
The university publishes lists or inventories of approved, prohibited or reviewed AI tools.
The university does not authorize licensing or sharing its data or intellectual property with external entities for AI purposes, and AI agreements need General Counsel review.

P66.sentence: Instructors should word AI policies with care: welcoming, explanatory and non-punitive in tone, in plain language and without anthropomorphic wording.
Instructors should discuss their AI policy and expectations with students in class at the start of the course, beyond the written syllabus.
Instructors should explain to students the reasons behind their AI rules, including why AI is allowed, limited or prohibited.
Instructors should discuss with students the ethical implications, risks, limitations and biases of generative AI.
Policies state that clear expectations, explanation and discussion help students understand AI rules, reduce confusion and support learning and integrity.
Instructors should explain the purpose of assignments and learning goals, and why doing the work themselves matters for students' learning.
Instructors should discuss academic integrity and plagiarism with students, including what counts as a violation when AI is involved.
Instructors should invite students' questions and open dialogue about AI and the policy, and make space for students to respond.
Instructors should state clearly what AI use is allowed and not allowed, with specific examples, and how use will be handled.
Instructors may use optional activities such as sharing considerations, debates, scenarios or short comments to start AI conversations with students.
Students are encouraged to ask questions, discuss expectations and reflect on the ethics of AI use.
When AI misuse arises, instructors should respond with supportive, transparent conversations with students before formal action.
Instructors should keep reminding students of the AI policy and keep discussing it throughout the semester, not only at the start.
Institutions should support open, ongoing dialogue about AI and its risks and impacts among faculty, students and the community.

P67.sentence: Instructors should co-create the course's AI policy, norms or guidelines with their students.
Instructors may co-create AI expectations or guidelines with students, or invite student negotiation and collaboration, if they choose.
Policies describe examples and resources where instructors discuss appropriate AI use with students or co-design AI-related work.
Instructors should hold an initial class discussion with students on responsible AI use, and encourage students to propose guidelines.
The class must co-create a class agreement on AI use with students early in the semester.
Policies state that involving students in policy development builds understanding, goodwill, trust and buy-in.

P68.sentence: Course policies state that their purpose is educational, not punitive, and that misuse is a chance to learn and adapt.
Instructors should encourage students to ask for extensions when struggling, to reduce pressures that lead to cheating.
Conduct and integrity processes are educational and supportive, so most first reports lead to educational outcomes, reminders or reflection rather than formal charges.
Instructors should talk with the student in an open, supportive, education-focused way, explaining the concern and assuming good faith rather than accusing.
Instructors should treat suspected or confirmed AI misuse, especially first offenses, as a teachable moment for learning and reflection rather than only discipline.
Instructors should offer the student a chance to revise, rewrite, redo or resubmit the work after suspected misuse.
Instructors should respond to violations with fair, educative and remedial sanctions and mild intervention for initial occurrences, not merely penalties.
Instructors can establish progressive remedial steps that give students prevention, clarification and corrective intervention before formal disciplinary action.
The university should develop and deploy educational modules to help students who commit violations.
Instructors should adopt a teaching-oriented, proactive rather than punitive approach to AI in general, before any misuse occurs.
Educators' primary work is to support students' development and foster exploration rather than to surveil, discipline or punish them; the policy is not meant to be punitive.
The university should avoid highly restrictive and punitive rules on generative AI use.

P69.sentence: Instructors should be able to show students knew the course rules, and departures from stated restrictions can be evidence of violations.
Instructors should not rely on AI detection results as the sole evidence of misconduct or the sole basis for a decision.
AI detection tool results must not be the sole evidence or basis for finding academic misconduct.
Instructors may gather evidence such as drafts, revision histories, process evidence, conversations with the student and course materials.
Policies state that detector output alone is insufficient to find a student responsible and does not determine responsibility.
Detector results may be used as supporting or preliminary evidence alongside other evidence, as part of a broader case.
Instructors should use multiple forms of evidence and a holistic approach when evaluating possible AI misuse.
Academic consequences and cases should rest on clear, documented evidence of a violation.
Instructors should review and verify suspected cases carefully and objectively, with human analysis, before reporting or taking action.
Policies set the standard of proof for misconduct findings, such as clear and convincing or more likely than not.
Suspicion that a student used AI is not sufficient to find misconduct or assign a grade.
Instructors should judge suspected misuse using course expectations, assignment requirements, student work and context.
Policies state that no single indicator, score or artifact establishes AI use or authorship.
Instructors may use plagiarism or AI detection tools.
Policies warn that AI detection tools are not fully accurate or reliable indicators of AI use.
The burden of proof in academic misconduct cases lies with the university.

P70.sentence: The institution provides AI training and professional development for faculty and staff.
The institution should build AI literacy into curricula, courses and learning outcomes across disciplines.
The institution should require students to take AI literacy courses, workshops or orientation.
Instructors should share or recommend AI literacy modules, resources and trainings with their students.
Instructors should teach students how AI works, its limits, and its ethical and responsible use.
Instructors and staff may help students learn about AI through hands-on activities and demonstrations.
Policies describe AI courses, workshops, modules and resources the institution offers to its community.
Policies state that AI literacy is an essential skill that students, faculty and staff need to develop.
The institution should provide training, workshops and support so students, faculty and staff understand and use AI responsibly.
Policies point students to guides, tutorials and courses for learning about generative AI and using it responsibly.
Community members are encouraged to attend AI training, workshops and use available AI resources.
Students should seek out training and learning opportunities to build their AI literacy.
All students, faculty and staff must complete required AI training, often every year or at onboarding.
Institutions state their commitment to fostering AI literacy across their community.
Completion of AI training may be required before people are given access to certain AI tools.

P71.sentence: Employees and meeting participants must promptly report AI concerns, problems, or issues to the host, IT, or the designated office.
Instructors must report discrepancies or issues with AI tools to IIT or the University AI Committee.
Everyone must immediately report suspected data breaches, security incidents, or unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data involving AI tools to the designated IT or security office.
Everyone should report suspected security issues, misuse, or ethical and compliance concerns about AI use through the proper university channels.
Everyone must report conduct that violates AI policy, and failing to report a known violation is itself a violation.
The university must provide channels for reporting, complaints and redress, and receive and review the reports.
The university must activate incident response, document and investigate incidents, notify affected parties and regulators, and refer violations to the proper bodies.
Students must report unethical AI use or AI misinformation and hallucinations to their instructor or supervisor.
Policies note that students may need to take further action together with their instructor or supervisor after reporting.
Researchers must report adverse events or unanticipated problems to the IRB.
Anyone may report AI-related risks, issues, or concerns through a university form, anonymous tool, or office.
Users must report AI tool malfunctions, vulnerabilities, or performance and accuracy problems to the designated office or incident database.

P72.sentence: Universities should provide students and advisors with contact information, resource lists and a designated referral point for human assistance.
Instructors should connect students to library, writing, tutoring and other academic support resources and remind them of these resources.
Students should reach out to instructors, librarians, writing centers or academic support services for help with their work, including before turning to AI.
Academic integrity questions and suspected misuse about AI go to conduct, honor code or student rights offices.
Students can get help from writing centers, tutoring, librarians, advisors and instructors, which are available resources.
Questions about AI security, privacy, compliance, tools or data should be directed to IT, information security or the CISO.
Questions about AI policy should be directed to designated university officials, offices or committees.
Users should contact a librarian to confirm citations, licensed content, copyright or whether a resource may be uploaded to AI.
Students should check with instructors or advisors about course policies and their use of AI.

P73.sentence: AI-assisted decisions must include human review, approval, and oversight by qualified people who can override the AI output.
Keep a human in the loop for important decisions, and AI should support rather than replace human judgment.
AI must not be the sole basis for, or independently make, consequential decisions about individuals such as admissions, academic standing, or discipline; meaningful human review is required.
Humans must retain final decision-making authority, accountability, and responsibility for decisions, which cannot be delegated to AI.
Policies state that AI supports and does not replace human judgment and decision-making.
AI should not be used for recruitment, personnel, or disciplinary decision making.
AI must not be used to make final personnel, hiring, or employment decisions.
AI must not replace human judgment, critical thinking, or professional judgment.

P74.sentence: Nobody may use AI to create or distribute malware, phishing or other malicious content, or upload data that helps do so.
Students must not use AI to fabricate or falsify data, results, sources, citations or other evidence in their work.
Students must not use AI to hide plagiarism, evade detection, or mislead others about where their work came from.
Nobody may use AI to generate or spread misinformation or false or misleading content.
Instructors must not misrepresent AI-generated content as original work.
Students must be careful to avoid unintentional plagiarism or data fabrication when using AI.
Instructors and researchers may use AI to produce deceptive content for pedagogical or research purposes when done intentionally.
Policies warn that submitting fabricated data, counterfeit citations or misinformation through AI is misuse.
Nobody may use AI to create discriminatory, defamatory, harmful or obscene content.
AI must not be used for illegal, fraudulent or unlawful activity.
Nobody may use AI to harass, bully, stalk, intimidate or sexually exploit others.
Nobody may use AI to threaten, bypass or gain unauthorized access to university systems, security or controls.
People should avoid using AI to deceive, mislead, manipulate or misrepresent.
Everyone must not use AI to fabricate, falsify or alter data, research results or academic content.
Everyone must not use AI to deceive, mislead or misrepresent others, and deepfakes must not be used fraudulently.
AI tools should not be used to fabricate, falsify or misrepresent information.
Nobody may use AI to create false or forged records, such as academic records, recommendations or medical excuses.
Nobody may use AI for unauthorized surveillance, monitoring or collection of personal information about individuals.
Policies warn that AI can be used to deceive, spread misinformation, or harm people and the university's work.
AI tools must not be used to facilitate academic dishonesty or give an unfair advantage.
Nobody may use AI to impersonate real people, including instructors, students or others, through text, images, audio or video.
People should avoid generating or sharing harmful, offensive or misleading content with AI, including deepfakes.
Policies warn that AI can access, manipulate or disrupt university systems.

P75.sentence: Everyone should stay vigilant against phishing schemes that exploit passwords, emails and other sensitive information, and when interacting with AI tools.
Everyone should use safe computing practices, such as caution with links and good antivirus protection, when working with AI.
Everyone should report suspicious messages and communications to the designated IT or security office.
Policies state that generative AI makes it easier for malicious actors to create sophisticated phishing emails, scams, deepfakes and other cybersecurity threats.
Everyone should stay vigilant against AI-enabled phishing attacks and scams, and be aware of how generative AI can be exploited.
Everyone must report suspicious or questionable messages and emails to the designated IT or security office.
Everyone should be cautious of deceptive or fake AI-generated images, videos and audio, and when creating or altering them.

P76.sentence: Administrators should develop frameworks, policies, guidelines and expectations for AI use in university operations and ensure proposals are reviewed and governed.
Staff must check with or consult their supervisor before using AI tools or new AI uses in their roles.
Staff and units may use generative AI for routine administrative and operational tasks such as drafting emails, summarizing meetings, scheduling and automating routine work.
AI-generated content and outputs for official use must be reviewed by a human before being sent, published or used.
Public-facing and official communications and materials must follow university communications standards and approval processes.
Policies note that safety and surveillance guidelines would benefit from attention to AI-enhanced systems.
Staff and administrators are encouraged to use or explore AI to improve efficiency, administrative processes and decision-making.
Universities support and describe AI efforts to improve efficiency in administrative and student service operations.
Administrators may use AI in institutional functions such as student services, advising, retention, decision-making and operations, subject to authorization or respect for privacy.
Staff should be transparent about how they use AI tools in their work.
AI should not be used for sensitive administrative functions such as legal advice, facial recognition security, vendor bid review or financial and HR projects.

P77.sentence: Instructors must align their course AI policies and syllabi with university policies and academic integrity rules.
Administrators must ensure AI systems, units' policies and implementation comply with laws and existing university policies.
Students should familiarize themselves with university and course AI policies before using AI tools.
Students should keep university academic integrity, conduct and technology policies in mind and use AI lawfully and honestly.
Instructors must follow FERPA, privacy and university policies when using AI.
Students must comply with privacy, data protection, FERPA, HIPAA and export laws when using AI.
Users must follow copyright and intellectual property laws when using AI.
Policies warn that AI use can create public records or violate law and policy, bringing disciplinary or legal consequences.
All users must comply with existing university policies and applicable laws when using AI.
Policies state that existing university policies and laws continue to apply to AI use and are not replaced by AI guidance.
Users should follow university policies, laws and ethical standards when using AI.
Students must follow the university's academic integrity policy, honor code, student conduct code and course rules when using AI.
Everyone must follow university data privacy, information security, IT acceptable use and data governance policies when using AI.
AI must not be used in ways that are illegal or that violate university policy or academic integrity.
Policies state that university AI policy is required by, aligned with or subordinate to state, system or board regulations.
Staff must use AI in compliance with institutional guidelines, export rules and applicable policy.

P78.sentence: Instructors and staff should share academic integrity policies with students and align with instructor guidance on AI.
Students should read each course syllabus and assignment instructions to learn what AI use is allowed.
Students are responsible for understanding and following the AI expectations of each course.
Students should ask or consult their instructors to clarify AI expectations when they are unsure.
Policies state that AI rules and expectations differ between courses and instructors.
Students must follow the AI rules their instructor sets for the course.
Students should check the assignment-specific instructions on AI use, in addition to the syllabus.
Students must not use AI when the instructor prohibits it or beyond the limits the instructor sets.
Policies state that not knowing or not clarifying the rules is not an excuse for a violation.
Students must understand and follow the university, school, program and departmental AI guidelines.
Students are responsible for using AI ethically and for knowing what is permitted, as these policies describe.
Everyone should follow the AI guidelines set by their institution, dean, instructor or supervisor.

P79.sentence: Instructors may require students to use AI in assignments or design activities that build in AI use.
Instructors should design assignments and courses that incorporate AI tools.
Instructors should assign tasks where students critically evaluate, critique or improve AI output.
Instructors should require AI only when necessary, state how it is used, and follow local requirements.
Instructors may let students choose between completing an assignment with or without AI.
Departments may include AI components in capstone courses.
Students must use generative AI to complete some assignments or tasks, as specified by the instructor.
Policies state that AI will be used, integrated or explored in the course and its assignments.
Students are expected to use AI tools in this course.
Instructors may have students critique, evaluate or compare AI output as an assignment.
Students may use AI when the instructor permits or asks for it in coursework.
Policies state that students are assessed on the value they add to AI output.

P80.sentence: AI governance bodies are appointed with set membership, which includes faculty, student and unit representatives.
Designated offices develop guidance, policies and protocols on AI use.
The institution should establish a standing AI committee or council with defined authority.
The institution must appoint or establish an AI governance committee or executive authority.
Units should designate AI leads, ambassadors or defined roles to coordinate AI work.
Instructors should review or discuss their AI policy with their dean, chair or program director.
Institutions may form an AI governance body or advisory council.
Instructors must get prior written approval from the program director before setting an individual course AI policy.
Students must get instructor approval for accommodations or exceptions to course AI rules, and should contact the instructor to discuss them.
Denials, disputes and unresolved questions are escalated to a named committee, leader or program head.
Academic misconduct involving AI is handled by the conduct office or instructor, who determine violations.
A named body reviews, updates and maintains the AI policy and guidelines over time.
Designated offices must review and audit campus procedures and AI use to monitor compliance.
Final authority to interpret the AI policy and decide on it rests with the president or governing board.
AI committees and councils provide oversight, strategy, advice, risk review and policy guidance.
IT, security or compliance offices are responsible for implementing and enforcing the AI policy.
The provost or academic affairs office is responsible for academic AI policy and standards.
Leaders and units must ensure their teams understand, implement and comply with the AI policy.
Exceptions to the AI policy must be approved by a designated office or committee.
A named office reviews and approves AI tools and maintains the list of approved tools.
Policies describe a process or contact point for requesting exceptions to the AI policy.

P81.sentence: Instructors should learn the reporting and student conduct procedures before misuse occurs.
The institution should establish and communicate procedures and guidelines for handling AI misuse.
Instructors must report suspected AI misconduct to the designated university office.
Instructors should report suspected AI misuse to the designated academic integrity or conduct office.
Instructors should handle suspected AI misuse through the institution's existing academic integrity or conduct procedures.
Policies state that reported AI violations are investigated and resolved by the designated office under existing integrity procedures.
Instructors may report suspected AI misuse to the conduct or integrity office, but reporting is optional.
Policies state that suspected AI misuse is reported to a named office and recorded as an integrity violation.
Instructors should include evidence, documentation and an explanation of the suspected violation in their report.
Instructors should consult the conduct office, honor committee or other designated contacts with questions about suspected misuse.
Instructors must submit the required report form within the stated deadline, one per violation.
Instructors should report promptly, including first-time or repeat offenses, so the university can record and track cases.
Instructors must follow the institution's formal procedures when AI misconduct is suspected.
Instructors may resolve concerns informally or impose an academic sanction under the applicable guidelines.
The designated office or dean must handle AI policy violations under the established procedures.
Instructors must not impose their own sanction or grade penalty before the deciding office makes a finding.
Instructors must notify the student of the allegation and gather evidence before submitting the report.
Instructors should not discuss the suspected violation with the student or their chair.
Instructors should not run student work through an AI detection tool.
Policies state that students may receive informal violations, which are not stored in the university database, and formal ones, which are.

P82.sentence: Instructors should not prohibit AI in their courses.
Instructors should help students learn to use AI responsibly instead of trying to ban it.
Policies warn that banning AI harms students by making work harder and cutting them off from useful technologies.
Policies warn that AI undermines the reliability of take-home work and other assessments of student learning.
Policies note that proctoring may reduce AI use in assessments.
Policies warn that AI use in student work is hard or impossible to detect or prove, and no detection method is foolproof.
Policies warn that detecting AI use will become harder as AI tools improve and as students learn to evade detectors.
Policies state that AI use cannot be fully prevented, and bans or prohibitions are impractical and hard to enforce.
Policies state that AI is already widely used and embedded in everyday tools, so students will use it regardless.

P83.sentence: Instructors should align their AI policy and permitted AI use with course learning objectives, without compromising them.
Instructors should start from their course learning objectives and outcomes, and reassess them, when deciding whether and how to allow AI.
Policies state that what AI use is appropriate depends on the course's learning objectives, since AI can help some goals and hinder others.
Instructors should weigh whether AI would support or hinder student learning in each course, task or assignment.
Instructors should identify the skills and knowledge students must practice or demonstrate without AI.
Departments, programs and institutions should jointly review and state learning outcomes in light of AI.
Instructors should tailor AI policies to their discipline and local course context.
Instructors should explain to students how the course's AI rules connect to the learning objectives.
Syllabus statements tell students the AI policy exists to protect and promote their learning and the course's learning goals.
Students must not use AI in ways that bypass or undermine the course's learning objectives.
Students should consider whether AI use is appropriate for their learning goals and justify it by relevance to them.
Students may use AI tools when the use aligns with or complements the course learning outcomes.
Instructors should return to and evaluate their AI policy and use over time.

P84.sentence: Policies state the purpose or scope of the policy effort: to build frameworks, principles, guidelines and resources for responsible AI use.
Policies state that the draft was shaped by consultation, feedback or public comment from faculty, students, staff and other stakeholders.
The university should establish baseline policies and general principles for generative AI use, including academic integrity guidelines.
Schools, instructors, students and stakeholder groups must have input into creating AI policies and guidance.
Policies state when the AI policy was first published, revised or updated, and what changed.
Policies state that the AI policy is interim or still under review, and that a fuller policy is being developed.
Policies state that a named committee, task force or working group, convened or charged by university leaders, drafted the AI policy or guidance.
Policies state which body approved, adopted, ratified or endorsed the AI policy, and on what date.
Policies disclose that generative AI tools were used to help draft, edit or refine the policy document.
Policies state that the guidance was adapted from or built on policies, frameworks or syllabus models from other institutions or groups.
Policies state that the document was written without generative AI assistance.

P85.sentence: Colleges, schools, departments and programs should develop their own AI guidelines or policies suited to their disciplines.
Units such as colleges, departments and programs may adopt their own more specific or additional AI policies, consistent with university policy.
Instructors should consult and follow their department, college or school AI guidelines and ensure their course policies are consistent with them.
Academic units must create their own AI policies or guidance and ensure they are consistent with university policy.
Instructors may set their own AI rules, and may vary from department policy if the variation is documented.
Instructors and others must comply with unit-specific guidance, and department or instructor policies must not conflict with university policy.
Policies state that colleges, schools or departments may have their own additional AI rules, guidance or expectations.
Policies state that AI expectations and appropriate use vary by discipline, so they are shaped locally within departments and units.

P86.sentence: Meeting hosts must obtain the consent of all participants before recording or transcribing with AI, and recording must not begin until everyone has consented.
Meeting hosts and participants must announce or give notice at the start that AI recording or transcription is active, as they would for any recording.
Students must obtain the instructor's permission before recording class sessions or lectures, including with AI tools.
Hosts must disable AI recording or transcription features when they are inappropriate or when a participant does not consent.
Do not use AI recording or transcription tools in confidential, sensitive or HR meetings, or allow unfamiliar bots to join meetings.
Participants should ask the host whether recording or AI transcription is enabled, and should decline to take part if the host insists on using these tools.
People must not create or distribute images, audio, video or likenesses of real people, including deepfakes, without their explicit consent.
Students may not use AI tools to transcribe, record, take notes on or summarize course lectures, unless approved as an accommodation.
Policies point to existing rules on recording classes and warn that AI recording raises privacy concerns and may violate wiretapping laws.
Students should have the right to attend classes without being recorded by AI tools.
Participants should balance productivity and convenience with respect for privacy and treat recordings as private among those who took part.

P87.sentence: Course statements tell students that responsible AI use can support and enhance their learning in the course.
Instructors should describe to students how generative AI use can enhance their learning.
Policies state that AI is a valuable, powerful tool that supports and enhances student learning.
Policies state that AI can help students understand concepts, summarize sources, practice, and improve their writing and coding.
Policies state that AI can personalize and adapt learning to each student's needs.
Policies state that AI saves time and raises efficiency and productivity by taking over routine tasks.
Policies state that AI can enhance teaching, learning, research and operations across the institution.
Policies state that AI can support instructors in course design, grading, content creation and teaching practice.
Policies state that AI has benefits for learning when it is used responsibly, appropriately and thoughtfully.
Policies state that AI can help students with disabilities, language barriers or special needs take part more fully and equitably.
Policies state that AI can foster creativity and innovation.
Policies state that AI can help students brainstorm and spark ideas at the start of work.
Policies state that AI can speed up research, discovery and data analysis.
Policies state that generative AI is transformative and will change how people teach, learn and research.
Policies state that AI can act as a tutor, giving students instant feedback, practice and round-the-clock support.
Policies state that the university wants to explore and embrace AI rather than ignore it.
The university should leverage AI to personalize learning and advance learning and creativity.
Policies recognize that generative AI brings both benefits and challenges.

P88.sentence: Universities benchmark and review the AI policies and practices of peer institutions when developing their own.
Policies describe ongoing campus-wide discussions, summits, and stakeholder forums on AI as a way to build shared understanding.
Universities should consult employers, alumni, and advisory boards and track workforce needs to keep AI guidance current.
Universities should build or join a coalition of peer institutions to help set shared standards for AI.
Universities should forge partnerships with industry, government agencies, and academic institutions to share knowledge and support AI work.
Universities should engage students, faculty, staff, and the broader community in discussions and forums on AI.
Faculty and staff should take part in university-wide conversations on AI and share effective practices and concerns.

P89.sentence: Instructors should ensure student work focuses on their own interpretation and critical analysis of AI results.
Instructors may define in course policies which AI data analysis uses are permitted.
Students may use generative AI to analyze data, find patterns and draw insights from it.
Anyone may use AI for data analysis, pattern recognition and visualization in research and coursework.
Students may use AI for calculations and spreadsheet manipulation only as specified in assignments.
AI use for data analysis is permitted only with oversight and under transparency policies.
Users should use extreme caution when using AI tools to analyze data.
Students must not use AI to analyze data, draw conclusions or interpret simulation results in graded work.
Policies state that AI advances research capabilities by automating data analysis.

P90.sentence: Students should do their own thinking, develop their ideas and attempt the assignment before turning to AI.
Students must write their own first draft or make an independent attempt before using AI, and must not use AI for that first draft.
Students may use AI to write, revise or summarize only after they have engaged with the work or materials themselves.
Instructors should introduce AI engagement only after students have done their own cognitive work, and ask students to edit their own work after using AI.
Students must not ask AI to outline, structure or generate solutions before developing their own approach.
Students may use AI for pre-task activities such as brainstorming, structuring and idea generation.

P91.sentence: Instructors may permit AI for editing, proofreading, grammar help or style adjustment in their course.
Instructors should decide and tell students whether AI editing tools are allowed in the course.
Students may use AI to check grammar, spelling and proofread their own writing.
Students may use AI to polish, revise and edit their own drafts for clarity, style and tone.
Students may use AI to outline, plan and organize their ideas.
Students may use AI as a general writing aid or assistant.
Students may use AI to format citations, references, bibliographies and documents.
Policies note that AI can help with editing and grammar, but it may rewrite text or fall short of other help.
Students must not use generative AI on writing assignments, including drafting or copy-editing.
Students are encouraged to use AI to proofread, outline, revise and edit their work.
Students must not use AI to generate, rewrite, restructure or make major revisions to their content.

P92.sentence: Instructors should choose and use approved or university-licensed AI tools, and check the approved list first.
Users should check with IT or get a review before adopting, purchasing or adding AI tools that are not already approved.
Instructors should not require students to create accounts with non-university AI tools that collect personal information.
Instructors should encourage or recommend that students use university-approved AI tools, and tell them where to find them.
Students should use university-approved or provided AI tools, signed in with their university account, rather than public or personal versions.
Everyone must use only university-approved or licensed AI tools, logged in with their university account.
